newsitem.title: CANADA: NBA BASKETBALL-NKOREAN BASKETBALL STAR HOPING TO MAKE NBA.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-NKOREAN BASKETBALL STAR HOPING TO MAKE NBA.

text.p: North Korean basketball star Ri Myong-Hun was expected to have a bright future in North America's National Basketball Association rather than a minor amateur league at home, his advisers said confidently on Tuesday.

Ri, known as Michael Ri in Canada where he was staying on a 90-day visitor visa, wants to be in the NBA. The 7'9" (236 cm) basketball star has been training every day with Jack Donohue, the former Canadian national coach, with an eye to making big bucks in the big league.

He has been living in an Ottawa hotel since May 13 and has bulked up to 280 pounds (127 kgs) from 234 pounds (106 kg). He works out daily with weights with the weight trainer for the National Hockey League's Ottawa Senators and works on basketball skills for two to three hours.
"I expect Michael to be in the NBA this year," Donohue told a packed news comference on Tuesday. "He should be at an NBA training camp, which opens in October."
Donohue, who once coached Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and is in the New York City Coaches Hall of Fame, was unequivocal in his praise of the North Korean giant.
"He's comfortable near the basket and you can see he's got good hands," said Donohue. "When he's away from the basket, he's as good as any of the NBA's big guys."
Donohue said he wanted to see Ri's weight increase to more than 300 pounds (136 kg) and become a bit more mobile.
"He's a quick learner. We showed him foot drills that we thought he'd have trouble with, but he picked them up right away," he said.
Ri, speaking through an interpreter, was often long-winded in his native tongue but the translations were remarkably short.
"I want to play in the NBA," was the answer to a question about when he first thought about pro basketball in the United States.
When the touchy subject of North Korean politics was raised, Ri gave brief answers or none at all.
When he was asked about his chances of being allowed into the United States, Donohue answered for him: "He knows nothing about the politics of him staying here."
Pressed to have Ri answer, Donohue asked, "Is it important for you to hear him say no comment?"

But the political situation means everything to Ri's NBA future. The United States does not recognise North Korea and the U.S. State department has told the NBA that its teams cannot talk to or negotiate with Ri.

Ri will undoubtedly apply for an extension of his visitor's visa to Canada, which expires in August, but whether he will be allowed in as a landed immigrant has not yet been addressed. He presumably could sign with the Toronto Raptors or the Vancouver Grizzlies of the NBA, but he would not be allowed to play games in the United States.

A similar situation occurred with Bob Probert, formerly of the NHL's Detroit Red Wings. Because of a drug conviction, if he went home to Canada, he would not have been allowed back. As a result, he played for the Red Wings only in the United States and missed the games in Canada.
Ri was asked how openly he can speak about conditions in North Korea, which was going through a severe famine and has had a terrible human rights record.
"There's nothing I can't say," he replied.
He also said that he liked Canada but will return home if he does not make it and what he does with his money is his business and no one else's.
"I"m here talking to you because I am tall. It is good to be tall. There is nothing bad about it," he said.
